Three risks worth fixing, in order of how likely they are to bite:

**1. `LazyFile.close()` keeps a dead handle — lines 166–169, with `close_intelligently()` 171–176 and `__exit__` 181–187**

`close()` closes `self._f` but never resets it to `None`. `open()` (148–164) short-circuits on `if self._f is not None: return self._f`, so once you close the file, or leave a `with` block, every later `open()` hands back the closed stream. Reuse raises `ValueError: I/O operation on closed file`, and `__getattr__` (140–141) proxies straight to that closed file. There is no path back to a working handle. Setting `self._f = None` in `close()` fixes it.

**2. `LazyFile.__getattr__` opens the file on any attribute read — lines 140–141**

Anything not defined on the class calls `self.open()`. So `hasattr(f, "x")`, `f.closed`, `f.fileno()`, `f.encoding` all perform real I/O, and a failed open raises `FileError` out of what reads like a plain attribute access. `__repr__` (143–146) avoids this by checking `_f` directly, which is the giveaway that the delegation is too broad. Proxy the handful of stream methods you actually need instead.

**3. `format_filename` can raise on the names it exists to make safe — lines 436–441**

The str branch does `filename.encode("utf-8", "surrogateescape").decode("utf-8", "replace")`. `surrogateescape` only maps U+DC80 through U+DCFF, so any other lone surrogate raises `UnicodeEncodeError` inside a function whose docstring promises the name "can be displayed". Windows filenames are UTF-16 and can carry unpaired surrogates, so this is reachable. The bytes branch on line 437 decodes with `sys.getfilesystemencoding()`, which is locale-dependent, so the same bytes render differently on different machines. Encoding with `"backslashreplace"`, or catching `UnicodeEncodeError`, closes both.
